notes: SCOPE ESTABLISHED FIRST: the passage is about this form and not a neighbour. Televantos printed 51, in the section 'How Effective Were Deed of Settlement Companies Created Using Trusts?', says of deed of settlement companies in terms that 'it was partnership law which meant that the company's assets were available to business creditors in priority to the separate creditors of shareholder-partners: the use of the trust made no difference'. That sentence IS AP1's question - priority of entity creditors over members' personal creditors in entity assets - asked of this form by name. The mechanism is set out at printed 22-23 (partners' rights of indemnity and lien; partnership creditors subrogated to them, Ex p Ruffin (1801)), restated at printed 145-46 and summarised at printed 167: 'the jingle rule, which ensured partnership assets would be distributed to partnership creditors in priority to the separate creditors of each partner'. ENTITY LOCATOR: the arrangement is the single undivided joint stock, reached from the sources and not from any project prose - printed 18, 'as partners were equitable co-owners of the firm's property, no partner could claim any particular asset of the firm as his own'; printed 37, the trustees held 'the circulating partnership assets'. No source describes internal sub-pools, so the sub-pool rule does not bite. NOT INDEPENDENT: Televantos cites Getzler & Macnair 2005 for the jingle rule itself (his n51), and glosses it as Hansmann-Kraakman-Squire 'soft' entity shielding (printed 146 n10), so this cell has ONE witness, not two, and its agreement with the framework AP1 is worded in is not corroboration. Getzler & Macnair reach the same rule in their section 'The Jingle Rule of Partnership Insolvency' (Craven v Knight, Ex p Crowder, Ex p Cook, Ex p Elton) - cited by section heading and case name only, because the bundle's copy is the Oxford working paper with no folio marks and no derivable offset - but they reach this form only by assimilation, and they source the assimilation to Harris 2000 (their n53). CONFIDENCE medium, NOT high, FOR A REASON IN THE SOURCE: no case applying the jingle rule to a deed of settlement company is reported. Televantos records at printed 47 n125 that 'creditors of deed of settlement companies did not sue out commissions of bankruptcy against them', and the jingle rule operated through commissions. The priority is asserted for this form, not demonstrated on one. ARTICULATION analyst-imposed: the period articulated the jingle rule for partnerships (Lord King C in Ex p Cook 1728) and articulated the assimilation (Gow 1823, printed 44 n99), but not the conjunction as a proposition about this form. UNAPPLIED QUALIFICATION, RECORDED AND NOT USED: at printed 144 Televantos says Hansmann, Kraakman and Squire 'overlook limitations on partnership law's ability to preserve business assets for business creditors' where a firm continued trading after a partner's death or retirement (Ex p Ruffin, printed 163-66). He does NOT apply that limitation to deed of settlement companies, and I have not carried it across; if it were evidenced for this form the cell would be P. See the adjudications in NOTES.

NOT RECORDED, AND THIS IS A RESULT ABOUT THE COLUMN'S SECOND LIMB. AP2 asks two things - that members cannot force partition or withdrawal, AND that MEMBERS' CREDITORS cannot - and the creditor limb is the whole of its increment over CI2. THE MEMBERS' LIMB IS WELL EVIDENCED FOR THIS FORM: the deeds excluded the default partnership rules (printed 36); vesting the assets in trustees 'was designed to insulate the company from the effect of the rules effecting mandatory partnership dissolution upon any change of partners' (printed 38); and shareholders 'could not easily use the courts to dissolve or withdraw their capital from such concerns' (printed 51), which 'de facto acted as a capital lock-in mechanism' (printed 52). Televantos qualifies even that: it 'was a by-product of what was, in effect, a rejection of jurisdiction over such companies, rather than a substantive rule of law' (printed 51), and he rejects Morley's reading of Van Sandau v Moore (1826) as designed to lock capital in - 'there is no hint of this in Lord Eldon's reasoning' (printed 50). THE CREDITOR LIMB IS NOWHERE ASKED OF THIS FORM. Neither source asks whether a shareholder's private creditor could force partition or withdrawal of a deed of settlement company's assets. The nearest passage, printed 148 - 'where a separate creditor of a partner levied judgment against that partner's share of the partnership assets, he could only claim the partner's right to the residue of the partnership assets after the partnership creditors had been paid' - is about ordinary partnership AND is about PRIORITY IN THE RESIDUE, which is AP1's question. Taking AP2 from it would fill this column out of a rich treatment of the other, and would make AP2 report AP1. Same for printed 166, 'A partner's separate creditors after all could have no better right to the partnership assets than he had.' The vocabulary's own rule governs: a source answering only the members' limb gives .NR here, not P. SPLIT TEST RUN, PER CHARACTER-CODING: a phase split of 1720-1844 would not give this cell a value in either phase, because what is missing is a question the sources never put, not a value that changes across the period. So the .NR is a claim about the evidence and not an evasion. WHAT WOULD MOVE IT: a source on execution or bankruptcy against an individual shareholder of a named deed of settlement company - see NOTES.

NOT APPLICABLE. AP4 applies ONLY where the entity was constituted by an endowment out of an identifiable founder's patrimony, and where there is no founder the cell is .NA and not 0. THE NO-FOUNDER FACT IS TAKEN FROM THE SOURCES AND NOT ASSUMED. Televantos's own glossary, printed 183, defines the form as 'a business which raised capital by issuing shares and/or bonds', 'distinct from a typical partnership, where the partners who managed the business provided the capital'; the constitutive act is a private deed drafted by counsel with company promoters (printed 36) and the capital is raised by subscription for shares (printed 36-37, 39, 45). That is constitution by SUBSCRIPTION, which the characteristic's definition names as one of the arising-modes that yield .NA. There is no corpus alienated by donation out of a named founder's estate anywhere in either source's treatment of this form. THE OUT-OF-SCOPE NEIGHBOUR WAS CHECKED AND EXCLUDED: the TESTAMENTARY TRADING TRUST at printed 53-60 IS founder-endowed - a trader settles his business assets on trustees by will - and it is a different form, expressly out of this batch's scope. Coding AP4 from that material would be coding the neighbour. .NA propagated through confidence, articulation, source_ref and source_lang, and source_read set to .NA on the census's majority practice for .NA rows (47 of 66).

source_ref: Televantos 2020, 44-46, quoting R v Dodd (1808) 9 East 516, 527
notes: OBSERVED ABSENCE, NOT SILENCE, AND ASKED OF THIS FORM BY NAME. Televantos gives the question a section of its own - printed 44-46, section 2.2.1 'Unlimited Liability of Shareholders' - and answers it: 'Shareholders of a deed of settlement company were in law partners of the firm, and this meant that they were personally liable without limit for the firm's debts' (printed 44). ARTICULATED: the period says it in its own idiom about this form, quoted verbatim. R v Dodd (1808) 9 East 516, 527 concerned the shareholders of a large deed of settlement company, and Lord Ellenborough CJKB held: 'As to the subscribers themselves, indeed, they may stipulate with each other for this contracted responsibility; but as to the rest of the world it is clear that each partner is liable to the whole amount of the debts contracted by the partnership' (Televantos printed 46). LOCATOR: AP3's locator is labour-party where CF1 is 1 or P and reverts to members otherwise. This form is not a bilateral capital-labour contract - the shareholder-partners subscribe capital and 'would have no individual powers of management over the concern' (printed 37), control lying with directors, a general court and trustees - so there is no labour-supplying party and the locator is members, who are alike. CF1's own cell was withheld with the rest of this form's rows and could not be read; FLAGGED FOR THE MAINTAINER. THE CONTRARY READING IS RECORDED RATHER THAN SUPPRESSED: John Morley (2016) argues the trust DID create limited liability for shareholders, only the trustees being liable. Televantos meets it at printed 45-46 with Hankey v Hammock (1786) and R v Dodd, and concludes the trust 'could not protect shareholders from liability for the firm's debts'. AP3 has no 'mixed' value, so the dispute is carried here and in NOTES, not in the value. Confidence medium for that reason. WHY NOT P: deeds sometimes contained limited-liability clauses, but 'such clauses were not fully effective' (printed 45) - their effect was only that a shareholder could demand the company's property be exhausted first, a benefit of discussion and not a shield, and creditors could then sue shareholders personally unless that individual creditor had agreed otherwise. A single creditor's agreement is a contract with that creditor, not a feature of the form. SPLIT TEST RUN: no phase split is available inside 1720-1844 - Televantos puts the change at 1855 and after - and the attribute does NOT turn on the individual instrument at every date, because his finding is precisely that variation in drafting made no difference to the legal position. That is why this cell is 0 and not .NR. OUT-OF-SCOPE NEIGHBOUR EXCLUDED: printed 53-60 shows trusts creating genuinely limited-liability trading entities - but those are TESTAMENTARY TRADING TRUSTS, and printed 60 warns 'it would be dangerous to draw this conclusion from deed of settlement companies alone because they were seen as partnerships'. No part of this cell comes from that section.

EXTENT AND FORM OF MEMBERS' LIABILITY TO THIRD PARTIES. EXTENT - unlimited - is articulated for this form in R v Dodd (1808), Lord Ellenborough CJKB: 'as to the rest of the world it is clear that each partner is liable to the whole amount of the debts contracted by the partnership' (Televantos printed 46), and stated at printed 44. FORM - joint, not several - is the express subject of a chapter section of its own: Televantos ch 7 section 4, 'Rule IV: Joint Creditors Have Rights against the Partners' Jointly, not a Firm' (printed 149), with 'creditors of the firm would acquire rights against partners jointly' at printed 144. IT IS CARRIED TO THIS FORM BY TWO FORM-SPECIFIC DATA, not by assimilation alone: (i) in Van Sandau v Moore (1826) a deed of settlement company could 'frustrate Chancery suits brought against it by insisting that in such litigation each of the partner-shareholders be added as defendants' (printed 50), which is the joinder consequence of joint and not several liability; and (ii) Lord Eldon's 1824 proposal that creditors of such companies 'should be able to recover the full amount of any debt by suing only some of the partner-shareholders' (printed 45 n108) presupposes that they could not. ARTICULATION analyst-imposed: the extent limb is articulated verbatim, but the compound value - unlimited AND joint - as a proposition about this form is assembled here from a quotation on extent and a procedural case on form. CONFIDENCE medium accordingly. LOCATOR: as at AP3, members and not labour-party; CF1 was withheld with this form's rows and the antecedent was resolved from the sources instead. FLAGGED. NOT INDEPENDENT: Getzler & Macnair's section 'Corporations' reaches the same result - deed of settlement companies 'were in the eye of equity, for the purposes of account, set-offs and liability to outsiders, seen as nothing more than a form of partnership', discussing Gibson v Hudson's Bay Company (1725) and Meliorucchi v Royal Exchange Assurance (1728) - but they source that assimilation to Harris 2000 (their n53), so they are not a second witness. Cited by section heading and case name only, because the bundle's copy carries no folio marks. 'none' AND 'limited' WERE BOTH CONSIDERED AND REJECTED: 'limited' on the ground that deeds purporting it were ineffective (printed 45), 'none' because liability plainly existed.
